title: A table of vectors
objectives: Explain an embedding as a table of vectors, and a one-hot product as a row lookup.

screens.title: A one-hot row times the table
screens.prose: Name it: an **embedding** is a table $\mathbf{E}$ with one row per item (makemore called it $C$). Here 4 items have 3 numbers each. Multiply the one-hot row of item 2 by $\mathbf{E}$.

state.caption: Items are numbered from 0, so item 2 is the third row.

screens.question: Fill in the product, a row of 3 numbers.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each entry is the one-hot row times a column of $\mathbf{E}$; only one term is not 0.

byKey.col: You read down column 2 of the table. The product picks out a row.
byKey.row1: You counted rows from 1. Item 2 is the third row, since items start at 0.

hints.text: Entry 1 is $0 \times 0.2 + 0 \times 1.5 + 1 \times (-0.7) + 0 \times 0$.
Every entry keeps only row 2: $(-0.7, 0.8, 2)$.

explain.text: The one-hot row has a single 1, in place 2, so each entry of the product is the matching entry of row 2. Multiplying by a one-hot vector is a lookup.

screens.title: Lookup by index
screens.prose: `E[i]` gives the same row with no arithmetic: it copies the numbers. The product spends a multiplication on every entry of $\mathbf{E}$, almost all of them by 0.

state.caption: 4 × 3 = 12 multiplications for 3 numbers that were already there.

screens.question: A word table has 50,000 rows and 300 columns. How many multiplications does one one-hot product take?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The one-hot row meets every entry of the table once.

byKey.copy: 300 is what the lookup copies. The product multiplies every entry of the table.
byKey.rows: That is one multiplication a row. Each row has 300 entries.

hints.text: One multiplication for each entry of $\mathbf{E}$.

explain.text: The product costs $50{,}000 \times 300 = 15{,}000{,}000$ multiplications and gives the same row as the lookup. So code uses `E[i]`, and the product stays as the way to reason about it.

screens.title: Only the rows used
screens.prose: A batch looks up items $(2, 0, 2)$. The loss's gradient for the three looked-up rows is the table $\mathbf{G}$ on the right. Backward hands each share to the row it came from.

state.caption: Lookups in order: item 2, item 0, item 2.

screens.question: Which rows of the gradient for $\mathbf{E}$ are not zero? Select all that apply.

options.text: Row 0
Row 1
options.why: Item 1 was never looked up, so no share of the gradient reaches row 1.

options.text: Row 2
Row 3
options.why: Item 3 was never looked up, so row 3 stays at zero.

feedback.correct: Rows 0 and 2. Row 2 was used twice and gets both shares added.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A row gets gradient only if the batch looked it up.

byKey.r1: You gave row 1 a gradient, but the batch never used item 1.
byKey.r3: You gave row 3 a gradient, but the batch never used item 3.

hints.text: Which items appear in $(2, 0, 2)$?
Items 0 and 2. Rows 1 and 3 get nothing.

explain.text: Row 0 gets $(0.5, 0, -0.1)$ and row 2 gets $(0.1 - 0.4, -0.2 + 0.6, 0.3 + 0.2) = (-0.3, 0.4, 0.5)$. Rows 1 and 3 stay at zero, so a step leaves them where they are.

screens.title: How wide
screens.prose: The width is a choice. Two columns let us draw the table; makemore's model used 10. Mikolov and colleagues' word2vec (2013) learned 300 numbers for each of about 3 million words and phrases.

state.caption: Width of one row, on a log scale.

screens.question: How many million numbers does the word2vec table hold?

feedback.correct: 3 million rows times 300 numbers is 900 million numbers.

byKey.width: 300 is the width of one row. There are 3 million rows.
byKey.rows: 3 million is the number of rows. Each holds 300 numbers.

hints.text: One row of 300 for each of 3 million words.
$3 \times 300$ million.

explain.text: $3 \times 300 = 900$ million numbers. Width trades how much each row can say against how much data it takes to learn it.

screens.title: Spin the table
screens.prose: A colleague reads column 3 of makemore's trained $27 \times 10$ table as a vowel score and wants to report it. Spin the table: replace $\mathbf{E}$ by $\mathbf{E}\mathbf{R}$ for a rotation $\mathbf{R}$, and give the first layer the reverse turn $\mathbf{R}^\top$.
screens.question: The model's dev loss was 2.1609. What is it after the spin?

options.text: 2.1609: every output of the model is unchanged
Higher: the rows have moved away from what was learned
options.why: The rows moved, but the first layer turned back by the same amount, so every hidden unit sees the same numbers.

options.text: It cannot be known without training again
options.why: No training is needed: the spin cancels inside the first layer, so the loss can be worked out exactly.

feedback.correct: Unchanged. The table's columns have no fixed meaning: a spun table with a spun first layer is the same model.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow one context into the first layer.

byKey.higher: You treated each column of the table as a fixed property that the spin destroyed. The layer undoes the spin, so nothing the model computes moves.

hints.text: The first layer multiplies the looked-up row by its weights.
$(\mathbf{e}\mathbf{R})(\mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{W}) = \mathbf{e}\mathbf{W}$, since $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{R}^\top = \mathbf{I}$.

explain.text: Each looked-up row meets the first layer as $(\mathbf{e}\mathbf{R})(\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{W}) = \mathbf{e}\mathbf{W}$, so the dev loss stays 2.1609. Column 3 of the spun table is a new mix of the old columns, so a vowel score read from it means nothing. The table is learned with the model, and only its geometry is fixed.

screens.title: A row that never trained
screens.prose: A model with a stock embedding was trained on last year's stocks. A company lists this year; its row was given a random start and has had no gradient since.
screens.question: What do the new stock's nearest rows in the table tell you?

options.text: Nothing yet: its row is still its random start
That it behaves like an average stock
options.why: A random start is not an average. Only training could have moved it towards similar stocks.

options.text: Which stocks it resembles
options.why: Its neighbours are whatever its random draw landed near. No data about it has touched the row.

feedback.correct: Nothing yet. A row learns only from batches that look it up.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which rows the gradient has reached.

byKey.near: You read its neighbours as learned. With no gradient yet, they come from the random start.

hints.text: Which rows does a backward pass change?
Only looked-up rows; this one has never been looked up in training.

explain.text: A row that no batch looked up keeps its random start, so its neighbours mean nothing. Until it has data, flag it or give it a stated default, such as its official sector's average row.

screens.title: A lookup is a product
screens.prose:
Stack the one-hot rows of a batch of lookups $i_1, \ldots, i_m$ as the rows of $\mathbf{H}$. Then

$$\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{E}[i_1] \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{E}[i_m] \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{E}} = \mathbf{H}^\top \mathbf{G}$$

where $\mathbf{G}$ holds the gradients of the looked-up rows.
screens.question: What does $\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{G}$ do with two lookups of the same item?

options.text: Adds their two gradient rows into that item's row
Keeps only the later of the two gradient rows
options.why: Column $i$ of $\mathbf{H}$ has a 1 in both lookups' places, so both rows of $\mathbf{G}$ enter the sum.

options.text: Averages the two gradient rows for that item
options.why: A product sums; nothing divides by the count.

feedback.correct: It adds them: column $i$ of $\mathbf{H}$ has a 1 for each use of item $i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Row $i$ of $\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{G}$ is column $i$ of $\mathbf{H}$ times $\mathbf{G}$.

byKey.last: You kept one use, as NumPy's `g[idx] += G` does. The product counts both.

hints.text: Row $i$ of $\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{G}$ sums the rows of $\mathbf{G}$ where column $i$ of $\mathbf{H}$ is 1.
Two uses put two 1s in that column, so two rows are added.

explain.text: Row $i$ of $\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{G}$ adds the gradient rows of every lookup of item $i$, and is zero for an item never looked up. It is the rule you used on the batch $(2, 0, 2)$, written as one product.

screens.title: The lookup and its gradient in code
screens.prose: Write `one_hot(idx, n)`, then `one_hot_lookup(E, idx)` as the product of the one-hot matrix and `E`. Then let the autograd find the gradient of `(E[idx] * dout).sum()` for `E`: wrap `E` in a `Tensor`, index it, call `backward()` and return its `grad`.
screens.question: Write `one_hot`, `one_hot_lookup` and `embedding_grad`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor


def one_hot(idx, n):
    H = np.zeros((len(idx), n))
    H[np.arange(len(idx)), idx] = 1.0
    return H


def one_hot_lookup(E, idx):
    E = np.asarray(E, dtype=float)
    return one_hot(idx, len(E)) @ E


def embedding_grad(E, idx, dout):
    T = Tensor(E)
    out = T[np.asarray(idx)]
    (out * np.asarray(dout, dtype=float)).sum().backward()
    return T.grad

import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor


def one_hot(idx, n):
    H = np.zeros((len(idx), n))
    H[np.arange(len(idx)), idx] = 1.0
    return H


def one_hot_lookup(E, idx):
    E = np.asarray(E, dtype=float)
    return one_hot(idx, len(E)) @ E


def embedding_grad(E, idx, dout):
    g = np.zeros(np.shape(E))
    g[np.asarray(idx)] += np.asarray(dout, dtype=float)
    return g

screens.title: Nearest rows
screens.prose: Write `nearest_rows(E, i, k)`: the indices of the $k$ rows closest to row $i$ by Euclidean distance, nearest first. Leave row $i$ out, and break a tie in favour of the earlier row. The file `makemore-mlp.json` holds makemore's trained table as `C`.
screens.question: Write `nearest_rows`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def nearest_rows(E, i, k):
    E = np.asarray(E, dtype=float)
    d = np.sqrt(((E - E[i]) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    d[i] = np.inf
    order = np.argsort(d, kind="stable")
    return [int(j) for j in order[:k]]

import numpy as np


def nearest_rows(E, i, k):
    E = np.asarray(E, dtype=float)
    d = np.sqrt(((E - E[i]) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    d[i] = np.inf
    order = sorted(range(len(d)), key=lambda j: (d[j], -j))
    order = np.array(order)
    return [int(j) for j in order[:k]]

import numpy as np


def nearest_rows(E, i, k):
    E = np.asarray(E, dtype=float)
    d = -(E @ E[i])
    d[i] = np.inf
    order = np.argsort(d, kind="stable")
    return [int(j) for j in order[:k]]
mutants.symptom: Ranks by the dot product, which favours long rows, instead of the distance.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Row $i$ is at distance 0 from itself: leave it out before sorting.
byKey.test-2: Rows 1, 2 and 3 tie at distance 1. A stable sort keeps them in index order.
byKey.test-3: Rows 0 and 2 are identical; row 2 is at distance 0 and must come first.

hints.text: Distances to row $i$: `np.sqrt(((E - E[i]) ** 2).sum(axis=1))`.
Set row $i$'s distance to `np.inf`, then `np.argsort(d, kind="stable")[:k]`.

explain.text: A stable sort of the distances gives the order, with ties in index order, once row $i$ is pushed to infinity. Level 2's next lesson asks whether distance is the right measure for rows of different lengths.

screens.title: A stock as an input
screens.prose: A return model takes a stock's identifier among 800 stocks. Fed in one-hot, the identifier meets a first layer of 64 units through $800 \times 64 = 51{,}200$ weights. Instead, look up an embedding of width 16 and feed that to the 64 units.
screens.question: How many weights do the embedding table and that first layer hold together, leaving out biases?

feedback.correct: $800 \times 16 + 16 \times 64 = 12{,}800 + 1{,}024 = 13{,}824$, about a quarter of the one-hot layer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the table to the layer behind it.

byKey.table: That is the table alone. The 16 numbers still meet 64 units: add $16 \times 64$.
byKey.onehot: That is the one-hot design. The embedding puts a 16-wide table in front.

hints.text: The table is $800 \times 16$; the layer is $16 \times 64$.

explain.text: $12{,}800 + 1{,}024 = 13{,}824$ weights. Each stock now has 16 numbers to learn from its own days instead of 64, and the 64-unit layer learns from every stock. A thinly traded stock needs far fewer days to settle a row of 16.

ideas: An embedding is a learned table $\mathbf{E}$ with one row per item; only distances and angles between rows carry meaning, so a spun table with a spun first layer is the same model.
A one-hot row times $\mathbf{E}$ picks out a row; `E[i]` gives the same row with no multiplications.
The gradient for $\mathbf{E}$ is $\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{G}$: rows looked up get their shares added, and every other row gets zero that step.

formula.name: Lookup and its gradient
formula.note: $\mathbf{H}$ stacks one one-hot row per lookup.
